THOUGHT: The patient is a 58-year-old white man with a 3-month history of a painless ulcer on the lower lip — a classic presentation for lip malignancy. Key risk factors are strongly present: chronic sun exposure (25 years as an outdoor fruit picker) and tobacco use (20 pack-years), both well-established independent risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lip, especially the lower lip. The lesion is located at the vermillion border — the most common site for lip SCC. Physical exam reveals a non-healing, non-tender ulcer without signs of resolution, raising concern for malignancy rather than benign causes (e.g., traumatic ulcer, aphthous ulcer, or infection). Critically, the biopsy demonstrates dysplasia and keratin pearls — histopathologic hallmarks of invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Keratin pearls indicate keratinizing differentiation, typical of well-to-moderately differentiated SCC. His comorbidities (hypertension, type 2 diabetes) do not explain the lesion but may influence surgical planning and wound healing. No features suggest alternative diagnoses (e.g., no induration or satellite lesions to suggest Merkel cell carcinoma; no systemic symptoms or lymphadenopathy to suggest lymphoma or metastasis; no vesicles or crusting to suggest viral or autoimmune etiology like pemphigus or lupus). Thus, the clinical presentation, high-risk exposures, and definitive histopathology converge on squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip.

DIAGNOSIS: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip
